content: Common sage, scientifically known as Salvia officinalis, is a small evergreen subshrub characterized by its woody stems, grayish leaves, and blue to purplish flowers. It is native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean region. This plant is widely cultivated for both culinary and medicinal purposes and is also referred to as garden sage, kitchen sage, or Dalmatian sage. In southern Europe, other related species are sometimes grown for similar uses, which can lead to confusion with common sage. Although this plant was originally the one referred to as sage, the name is now also applied to several related species. The applications and benefits of common sage are numerous and diverse, often overlapping with those of related species. Common uses include: Infusions, which are believed to have calming effects, soothe sore throats, and aid digestion. Preservative flavorings, such as in cheese. Culinary flavorings, for example, in sage and onion stuffing. Common sage is also cultivated in parts of Europe, particularly the Balkans, for the extraction of its essential oil. Other species, such as Salvia triloba, may also be harvested and distilled alongside it. Numerous cultivars of common sage exist, most of which are grown more for ornamental purposes than for their herbal properties. These cultivars are valued as small ornamental flowering shrubs and for ground cover, especially in sunny, dry locations. They are easily propagated from summer cuttings. Notable cultivars include: Purpurascens, a purple-leafed variety considered by some to be the strongest of the garden sages. Tricolor, with white, yellow, and green variegated leaves. Berggarten, known for its large leaves. Icterina, with yellow-green variegated leaves. Alba, a white-flowered variety. Lavandulaefolia, a small-leaved cultivar. Culinary Uses Sage is recognized for its slightly peppery flavor. In Western cuisine, it is commonly used to flavor fatty meats (often as a marinade), cheeses (e.g., Sage Derby), and certain beverages. In Britain and Flanders, sage is paired with onion for poultry or pork stuffing and is also used in sauces. French cuisine incorporates sage in the preparation of white meats and vegetable soups. In Germany, sage is frequently used in sausage dishes and is the dominant flavor in English Lincolnshire sausages. Sage is also a staple in Italian cooking, where it is sautéed in olive oil and butter until crisp, then served with plain or stuffed pasta (a dish known as burro e salvia). In the Balkans and the Middle East, sage is used when roasting mutton. Medicinal Uses The Latin name for sage, salvia, translates to to heal. While the effectiveness of common sage is often debated, it has historically been recommended for a wide range of ailments. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial found sage to be effective in managing mild to moderate Alzheimer’s disease. Active Constituents The most potent active components of sage are found in its essential oil, which contains cineole, borneol, and thujone. Sage leaves also contain tannic acid, oleic acid, ursonic acid, ursolic acid, cornsole, cornosolic acid, fumaric acid, chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, niacin, nicotinamide, flavones, flavone glycosides, and estrogenic substances. Applications Internal Use: Sage is used to address indigestion, gas, liver complaints, excessive lactation, excessive perspiration, excessive salivation, anxiety, depression, female infertility, and menopausal issues. External Use: It is applied for insect bites, throat and mouth infections, gum issues, skin infections, and vaginal discharge. Health Precautions Sage can be toxic if consumed in excessive amounts or over prolonged periods. It is contraindicated during pregnancy and for individuals with epilepsy. Source: The Herb Society of America New Encyclopedia of Herbs & Their Uses by Deni Bown (New York: DK, 2001).
